topic.subject: science

note.title: Antibiotics, antibiotic resistance and vaccination
note.subject: science

mustKnow: Antibiotics (penicillin) are chemicals produced by fungi that kill bacteria or reduce their growth; they do not work on viruses
Largest clear zone = most effective antibiotic: say it with the comparison
Higher: overuse of antibiotics leads to resistance and superbugs such as MRSA; hygiene, isolation and fewer prescriptions reduce them
Vaccines use modified pathogens to raise antibody and memory lymphocyte levels
Higher: boosters raise the levels again; read the antibody graph against the level needed for immunity
Mean = (sum of repeats) ÷ number of repeats, with brackets on a calculator

notOnThisSpec: Herd immunity (other boards teach it here; CCEA's statements do not mention it)
Painkillers, and the full drug-development pathway with placebos and double-blind trials
How each class of antibiotic works inside the cell, beyond the wall damage a diagram may show
The MMR schedule and named national vaccination programmes

mustBeAbleTo: State that antibiotics, for example penicillin, are chemicals produced by fungi that kill bacteria or reduce their growth
Explain why antibiotics do not work against viral diseases such as colds, flu and HIV
Compare antibiotics from clear zones, using the largest zone and quoting the evidence from the plate
Find the minimum effective concentration from a plate of discs, and say why it matters
Calculate a mean clear zone from repeats, with brackets, and check it lies between the repeats
Higher Tier: explain how overuse of antibiotics leads to resistant bacteria and superbugs such as MRSA, as natural selection
Higher Tier: give procedures that reduce superbugs in hospitals, a way to kill MRSA outside the body, and say why superbugs are difficult to eradicate
State that vaccines use modified pathogens to raise antibody and memory lymphocyte levels in the blood
Explain why a vaccinated person does not become ill: memory lymphocytes, antibodies faster, and more of them
Higher Tier: read an antibody graph against the level needed for immunity, and explain what a booster does
sheet.howExamined: B2, 1 hour 15 minutes, calculator allowed. Antibiotics usually arrive as short recall inside a disease question (name the drug for a bacterial infection) and, on Unit 7 Booklet B, as plates with clear zones: which antibiotic works best and why, in comparative words, and the minimum effective concentration (Summer 2019, 2023, 2025). Resistance and superbugs are Higher only: a diagram of a dish before and after an antibiotic, an MRSA graph with true, false or cannot-tell statements, and procedures to reduce spread (Summer 2023, 2024, 2025). Vaccination questions ask what the vaccine raises and why the second response is faster; Higher papers add an antibody graph with a booster (Summer 2021).
traps: Drawing or describing some non-resistant bacteria still alive after the antibiotic, and not being able to name a way to kill MRSA outside the body, such as alcohol gel, antiseptic or disinfectant (Summer 2025 B2 Higher Q7)
Reading the line for the wrong region or group when two are plotted on one graph, so two answers come out swapped (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q8)
Explaining a rise in resistance through immunity and antibodies, instead of resistant individuals surviving, reproducing and passing on the gene (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q9)

Choosing the right antibiotic but not saying it gave the largest clear zone and so killed the most bacteria, and answering from general knowledge of MRSA instead of from the plates in front of you (Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology Booklet B Higher Q3)
Not thinking carefully about the minimum effective concentration: it is the lowest concentration that still gives a clear zone (Summer 2023 Unit 7 Biology Booklet B Higher Q3)
Describing the second response vaguely, or in terms of the antibody's shape, instead of memory lymphocytes making more antibodies, faster (Summer 2025 B2 Foundation Q7 and Higher Q3)
Writing antibodies where the drug, an antibiotic, is meant (Summer 2023 B2 Foundation Q1)
Typing a mean without brackets, so the result is larger than every repeat (Summer 2024 Unit 7 Biology Booklet A Foundation Q1)
Saying the antibiotic made the bacteria resistant: the resistant ones were already there
Subtracting when a question asks how many times higher, and giving the week the level fell below the line as the number of weeks it stayed above it

workedExamples.stem:
A student measured the clear zone round discs of three antibiotics, P, Q and R, on plates of the same bacterium, three times each.
(a) Calculate the mean clear-zone diameter for antibiotic Q. [2]
(b) Which antibiotic was the most effective? Use the means to explain your answer. [2]

data.caption: Clear-zone diameters for three antibiotics against one bacterium

steps.decision: Add the repeats first, then divide by how many there are. On a calculator the brackets are not optional: without them only the last number is divided.
Check it lies between the smallest repeat, 21, and the largest, 24. A mean outside that range is always a slip.

options: A mean can never be smaller than the smallest value or larger than the largest
A mean is always a whole number
A mean is always the middle value
whyMenu.explain: An average sits among the values it is made from. That one fact catches the missing-brackets slip every time.

steps.working: means: P 13.0 mm, Q 23.0 mm, R 16.0 mm
steps.decision: Work out every mean the same way before comparing anything.

steps.working: Q: it has the largest mean clear zone, 23.0 mm, so it killed the most bacteria.
steps.decision: Name it, compare with a word ending in -est, and say what the zone means. 'A big clear zone' earns nothing, because all three have one.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) 23.0 mm. (b) Antibiotic Q: it has the largest mean clear zone, 23.0 mm, compared with 16.0 mm for R and 13.0 mm for P, so it killed the most bacteria.

twin.stem: Using the same table, calculate the mean clear-zone diameter for antibiotic R (repeats 17 mm, 15 mm, 16 mm). Give your answer to one decimal place.

workedExamples.stem:
The graph shows the antibody level in a person's blood after a first dose of a vaccine and a booster.
(a) Calculate how many times higher the peak after the booster is than the peak after the first dose. [2]
(b) Explain why the antibody level rose faster and higher after the booster. [3]

figure.alt: A graph of antibody level, in arbitrary units from 0 to 150, against time after the first dose, in weeks from 0 to 30, on a grid of small squares, one week wide, with a major line every 25 units up the side. A dashed horizontal line marks the level needed for immunity at 30. Arrows mark the first dose at week 0 and a booster at week 10. The curve rises to a small peak after the first dose and falls back, then rises steeply after the booster to a much higher peak and falls slowly.

steps.working: peaks read from the graph: 24 after the first dose, 120 after the booster
steps.decision: Read each peak at the top of its curve, straight across to the scale. Say what you read before you use it.
'How many times' is a division. 120 − 24 = 96 answers a different question: how much higher.

options: Because 'how many times' asks how many of the smaller fit into the larger
Because a subtraction would give a negative number
Because the booster always gives a whole number of times
whyMenu.explain: Dividing asks how many 24s make 120. A check that always works: 5 × 24 = 120.

steps.working: The first dose made memory lymphocytes, which stayed in the blood.
steps.decision: Start with the cells that were left behind: they are the reason for everything that follows.

steps.working: At the booster they recognised the antigens at once, so antibodies were produced faster and in far greater numbers.
steps.decision: Two separate marks here, faster and more: say both, in words the scheme uses.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) 5 times higher. (b) The first dose made memory lymphocytes, which stayed in the blood; at the booster they recognised the antigens at once, so antibodies were produced faster and in greater numbers.

twin.stem: Using the same graph, give the week after the booster in which the antibody level first rose above the level needed for immunity. Give the nearest whole week.

items.stem: Before we start, three things from earlier topics. You are not expected to know all of them yet. Which cells make antibodies?
items.skill: Recall the cells that make antibodies

options.feedback: Lymphocytes, a kind of white blood cell. Vaccines work through them.
Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens. The antibody makers are lymphocytes.
Red blood cells carry oxygen. Antibodies come from lymphocytes.
Platelets help blood clot. Antibodies come from lymphocytes.

items.stem: What type of pathogen causes flu?

options.feedback: A virus. Keep that in mind: it decides what can and cannot treat flu.
Flu is viral. The bacterial diseases on the specification are chlamydia, salmonella and tuberculosis.
Flu is viral. The fungal diseases are athlete's foot and potato blight.

items.stem: In natural selection, which individuals are most likely to survive and reproduce?

options.text: those best suited to their environment
options.feedback: The best-suited survive and pass on their alleles. Antibiotic resistance is the same idea, happening fast.
Size only helps if it suits the conditions. 'Best suited to the environment' is the idea.

options.text: those that try hardest to adapt
options.feedback: No organism chooses to adapt. Individuals that happen to be suited survive.
Age has nothing to do with it. The best-suited survive and reproduce.

options.text: A chemical made by fungi that kills bacteria or stops them growing
options.feedback: Exactly: penicillin, from a mould, is the classic example.

options.text: A protein made by white blood cells that sticks to antigens
options.feedback: That is an antibody. An antibiotic is a drug.

options.text: A weakened form of a pathogen that gives immunity
options.feedback: That is a vaccine.
Antibiotics do not affect viruses at all.

items.stem: Why are antibiotics no use against flu?
items.skill: Explain why antibiotics fail on viruses

options.text: Flu is caused by a virus, which antibiotics do not affect
options.feedback: Right: antibiotics act only on bacteria.

options.text: The flu bacteria are all resistant
options.feedback: Flu is not bacterial; it is caused by a virus.

options.text: Flu is too mild to need them
options.feedback: Even severe flu is not treated with antibiotics, because it is a virus.

options.text: The flu vaccine stops them working
options.feedback: Vaccines and antibiotics do not interfere. Flu is viral.

items.stem: Higher Tier. How does a population of bacteria become resistant to an antibiotic?

options.text: Resistant bacteria already present survive the antibiotic and reproduce
options.feedback: Selection, not change: the resistant ones were there first.

options.text: The bacteria make antibodies against the antibiotic
options.feedback: Bacteria have no immune system. This is natural selection, not immunity.

options.text: Each bacterium gets used to the antibiotic and changes
options.feedback: No individual changes. Resistant bacteria were already there, and the antibiotic removed the rest.

options.text: The antibiotic mutates the bacteria it touches
options.feedback: Mutations happen by chance, before the antibiotic. It only selects which bacteria survive.

items.stem: Higher Tier. What makes MRSA a superbug?

options.text: It is resistant to most antibiotics
options.feedback: That is the definition: most antibiotics no longer kill it.

options.text: It is a virus, so antibiotics cannot reach it
options.feedback: MRSA is a bacterium. It is resistant, not viral.

options.text: It cannot be killed by any chemical
options.feedback: Alcohol gel, antiseptics and disinfectants kill it outside the body; that is how hospitals control it.

options.text: It grows much larger than other bacteria
options.feedback: Size is not the issue. It is resistant to most antibiotics.

options.text: A modified form of the pathogen, such as a dead or weakened one
options.feedback: Enough to be recognised, not enough to make you ill.
The body makes its own antibodies in response. A vaccine contains a modified pathogen.
Antibiotics treat bacterial infections; they are not in vaccines.
Memory lymphocytes are made by your body after the vaccine, not put in by it.

items.stem: Higher Tier. Why is a booster vaccination given?
items.skill: Explain the role of a booster

options.text: To raise antibody and memory lymphocyte levels again as they fall
options.feedback: A booster tops the levels back up, usually well above the level needed for immunity.

options.text: To cure the disease if the first dose did not work
options.feedback: A booster prevents; it does not cure.

options.text: Because the first dose contained no antigens
options.feedback: The first dose did contain antigens; the levels it produced simply fall over time.

options.text: To kill bacteria that survived the first dose
options.feedback: Vaccines do not kill bacteria directly. A booster raises antibody and memory lymphocyte levels.

items.stem: Higher Tier. A dish holds mostly non-resistant bacteria and a few resistant ones. An antibiotic that kills every non-resistant bacterium is added. What will the dish hold 24 hours later?

options.text: Only resistant bacteria, and more of them than before
options.feedback: The antibiotic removed every non-resistant one; the resistant ones kept dividing.

options.text: Mostly non-resistant bacteria, with a few more resistant ones
options.feedback: An antibiotic that kills every non-resistant bacterium leaves none of them behind. Only the resistant ones remain, and they multiply.
The resistant bacteria are not killed, so they survive and multiply.

options.text: The same bacteria as before, now all resistant
options.feedback: No bacterium changes. The resistant ones were there from the start; the others were killed.

items.stem: Why is the second response to the same pathogen so fast?

options.text: Memory lymphocytes recognise it and antibodies are made quickly
options.feedback: Memory cells, faster, more: the three ideas every mark scheme looks for.

options.text: The antibodies have exactly the right shape for the antigen
options.feedback: They always do. What makes the second time faster is the memory lymphocytes.

options.text: The pathogen is weaker the second time
options.feedback: The pathogen is just as strong; the body is better prepared.
The memory belongs to memory lymphocytes.

Resistant bacteria are double circles; bacteria that are not resistant have a shaded centre, and those the antibiotic kills are crossed out. Generation 1: 2 resistant, 4 not resistant that survive the dose, 14 killed; Generation 2: 7 resistant, 3 not resistant that survive the dose, 10 killed; Generation 3: 14 resistant, 1 not resistant that survive the dose, 5 killed; Generation 4: 19 resistant, 0 not resistant that survive the dose, 1 killed.

hints: Count the double circles in generation 2, then divide by the size of the population.
parts.stem:
The diagram shows a population of bacteria treated with the same antibiotic, generation after generation.
Calculate the percentage of the bacteria in generation 2 that were resistant.

hints: Describe first (what happened to the percentage), then the three links: killed, survived, reproduced.

commonErrors.feedback: Bacteria do not have an immune system and do not make antibodies. Resistance spreads because the resistant bacteria survive the antibiotic and reproduce.

parts.stem: Describe and explain how the population changed over the four generations.

accepted: The percentage of resistant bacteria increased, from 10% to 95%. The antibiotic killed the non-resistant bacteria, the resistant bacteria survived, and they reproduced and passed on their resistance, so each generation had more resistant bacteria.

the antibiotic killed the bacteria that were not resistant

scheme.examinerNote: Immunity and antibodies earn nothing here: bacteria do not make antibodies. The mark is for survival and reproduction.

parts.workedSolution: The percentage of resistant bacteria increased, from 10% in generation 1 to 95% in generation 4. Each dose of the antibiotic killed most of the bacteria that were not resistant. The resistant bacteria survived, and they reproduced and passed on their resistance, so each new generation had a larger proportion of resistant bacteria.

hints: Look at generation 1, before any antibiotic had done anything.

parts.stem:
The graph shows the number of patients who developed MRSA while in two hospitals, A and B, per 10 000 patients. Hospital A began a hygiene and isolation campaign in 2018.
Use the graph: how many patients per 10 000 developed MRSA in hospital B in 2019?

scheme.for: 34 (accept within half a small square)

parts.workedSolution: 34 patients per 10 000.

hints: Fall first, then divide by the value you started from.

commonErrors.feedback: The fall was divided by the final value, 15, instead of the starting value, 42. A percentage change is always measured against where you started.
That is the fall in patients, 27. To make it a percentage, divide by the starting value, 42, and multiply by 100.

parts.stem: By what percentage did the number of patients per 10 000 developing MRSA in hospital A fall between 2016 and 2021? Give your answer to one decimal place.

Use only the graph. Is this statement true, false, or is it not possible to tell?
'From 2018 onwards, fewer patients developed MRSA in hospital A than in hospital B every year.'

options.feedback: True: from 2018 hospital A's line is below hospital B's in every year.
Check each year from 2018 to 2021: hospital A's line is below B's in all of them.
The graph shows both hospitals for every year, so this can be told.

scheme.for: True

parts.workedSolution: True.

parts.stem:
Use only the graph. Is this statement true, false, or is it not possible to tell?
'The campaign caused the fall in MRSA cases at hospital A.'

options.feedback: The fall came after the campaign began, but the graph cannot show that the campaign caused it; something else could have changed too.
The graph gives no evidence against it either. It cannot show cause at all.
Cannot tell: the graph shows the two happened together, not that one caused the other.

scheme.for: Cannot tell

parts.workedSolution: Cannot tell.

parts.stem:

'The number of patients developing MRSA in hospital B fell every year.'

options.feedback: Look at 2017 to 2018 on the dashed line.
False: hospital B's value rose between 2017 and 2018.
Every year is plotted, so it can be told.

scheme.for: False

parts.workedSolution: False: it rose between 2017 and 2018.

figures.alt: A graph of antibody level, in arbitrary units from 0 to 150, against time after the first dose, in weeks from 0 to 30, on a grid of small squares, one week wide, with a major line every 25 units up the side. parts.stem:
A lotion that kills head lice has been used in one area for many years. Scientists collected 1,600 head lice from children in the area and found that 1,187 of them were not killed by the lotion.
Calculate the percentage of the lice that were resistant to the lotion. Give your answer to two decimal places.

hints: The same four links as for bacteria and an antibiotic: mutation, killed, survived and reproduced, gene passed on.

commonErrors.feedback: Lice do not become immune and make no antibodies. This is natural selection: resistant lice survive the lotion, reproduce and pass on the gene.

parts.stem: Explain, in terms of natural selection, why nearly all the head lice in this area are now resistant to the lotion.

accepted: A mutation made a few lice resistant to the lotion. The lotion killed the lice that were not resistant, but the resistant lice survived and reproduced, and their offspring inherited the gene for resistance, so over many years most of the lice became resistant.

scheme.examinerNote: Lice do not become immune and make no antibodies: the marks are for survival, reproduction and the gene passed on.

parts.workedSolution: By chance, a mutation made a few lice resistant to the lotion. Each time the lotion was used it killed the lice that were not resistant, but the resistant lice survived and reproduced, and their offspring inherited the gene for resistance. Over many years the proportion of resistant lice grew until most of them were resistant.

context.setting: How a vaccine protects a person from a disease

hints: Tell it as a story in two halves: the injection, then the real infection months later.
The words that lift an answer are modified, antigens, lymphocytes, antibodies, memory lymphocytes, faster and more.

commonErrors.feedback: The fit between antibody and antigen is true but it is not the protection. The marks gather round memory lymphocytes and a second response that is faster and larger.

parts.stem:
Describe how a vaccine protects a person from a disease, from the injection to the day the real pathogen arrives.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: At least five of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; everything set out in a clear and sensible order; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

At least three of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; an order you can follow, though it is not held right through; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
At least one of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; ideas in an order that is hard to follow; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave what you meant unclear.

indicativeContent.point: the vaccine contains a modified form of the pathogen, such as a dead or weakened one
the person does not become ill from the vaccine
lymphocytes (white blood cells) recognise its antigens
memory lymphocytes are made and stay in the blood for a long time
when the real pathogen enters, the memory lymphocytes recognise it
in greater numbers, so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms appear

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] at least five points, Band B [3]-[4] at least three, Band C [1]-[2] at least one, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: Answers that describe how an antibody fits an antigen, without the memory lymphocytes and the faster, larger second response, cap at Band B: the question is about why the vaccinated person stays well. Higher Tier answers may add that a booster raises the antibody and memory lymphocyte levels again.

parts.workedSolution: The vaccine contains a modified form of the pathogen, for example a dead or weakened one, so the person does not become ill from it. Lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, recognise its antigens and produce antibodies against them. Memory lymphocytes are also made, and they stay in the blood for a long time. Months later, when the real pathogen enters the body, the memory lymphocytes recognise it at once. Antibodies are produced much faster than the first time, and in greater numbers, so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms appear.

findTheMistake.stem:
Aoife measured the clear zone round an antibiotic disc three times: 18 mm, 22 mm, 20 mm. She is asked: 'Calculate the mean clear-zone diameter. [2]'
Her working:
studentWorking: mean = total of the repeats ÷ number of repeats
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 was typed without brackets, so the calculator divided only the last repeat by 3. A mean of 46.7 mm is larger than every repeat, which is impossible.
correction: mean = total of the repeats ÷ number of repeats
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of two: the method in line 1 is right. Brackets put the division last. Then check: 20.0 mm lies between 18 mm and 22 mm, as a mean must.

findTheMistake.stem:
Seán is asked: 'Use the antibody graph to calculate how many times higher the peak after the booster is than the peak after the first dose. [2]'
His working:
studentWorking: peak after the first dose = 24 arbitrary units
peak after the booster = 120 arbitrary units
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 subtracts. 120 − 24 = 96 says how much higher the booster peak is, not how many times higher: 'how many times' is always a division.
correction: peak after the first dose = 24 arbitrary units
peak after the booster = 120 arbitrary units
findTheMistake.feedback: The two readings are right, but the method mark is for the division: 120 ÷ 24 = 5 times higher. A check: 5 × 24 gives back 120.

prompts.answer: A chemical made by fungi, such as penicillin, that kills bacteria or stops them growing.

prompts.prompt: Why do antibiotics not work against a cold or flu?
prompts.answer: Colds and flu are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only act on bacteria.

prompts.prompt: On an antibiotic plate, what does the largest clear zone tell you?
prompts.answer: That antibiotic killed the most bacteria, so it is the most effective: write 'largest clear zone'.

prompts.prompt: Higher Tier. How does overuse of antibiotics lead to superbugs?
prompts.answer: Resistant bacteria survive each dose, reproduce and pass on the gene, so the resistant proportion grows every time antibiotics are used.

prompts.prompt: Higher Tier. Give three procedures hospitals use to reduce superbugs.
prompts.answer: Hand hygiene with alcohol gel, isolating infected patients, and prescribing antibiotics only when needed.

prompts.prompt: What does a vaccine contain, and which two levels does it raise in the blood?
prompts.answer: A modified pathogen, dead or weakened; it raises the levels of antibodies and memory lymphocytes.

prompts.prompt: Why does a vaccinated person not become ill when the real pathogen arrives?
prompts.answer: Memory lymphocytes recognise it, so antibodies are made faster and in greater numbers.

prompts.prompt: Higher Tier. On an antibody graph, why is a booster given?
prompts.answer: The level falls, or never reaches the line; after a booster it rises faster and higher and stays above the line longer.

findings.asked: What a vaccine causes the body to make, and why a second exposure is dealt with faster.
findings.wentWrong: 'Antibodies' was known; the secondary response was described vaguely or as being about the specific fit of antibodies, rather than memory lymphocytes producing antibodies faster and in larger amounts.
findings.rule: Secondary response = memory lymphocytes, faster, more antibodies.

findings.asked: The same vaccination question at Foundation.
findings.wentWrong: Many gave the same vague or misdirected secondary-response answers.
findings.rule: Three ideas: memory cells, quicker, bigger.

findings.asked: Explain, in an unfamiliar predator-prey context, why resistance increased in a population, then give the advantage of the change to the other species.
findings.wentWrong: Natural selection is a topic candidates find difficult: a number drifted into immunity and antibodies instead of the passing on of advantageous genes, and too many gave the effect on the predator when the advantage to the prey was asked for.
findings.rule: Resistance in a population is natural selection - variation, survival, reproduction, allele passed on - not immunity.

findings.asked: Compare antibiotic clear zones and use them as evidence about MRSA.
findings.wentWrong: Picking the best antibiotic was easy, but the reason needed the evidence (largest clear zone, so it killed the most bacteria); a statement that one antibiotic was ineffective against both strains was often missed; and only the more able used the diagram rather than general knowledge about MRSA.
findings.rule: Every judgement from a practical needs the measurement that supports it.

insight.ruleToRemember: A vaccine contains antigens, so lymphocytes make antibodies and memory lymphocytes; on re-infection the response is faster and larger. Antibiotics kill bacteria (not viruses); resistance spreads because resistant bacteria survive and reproduce - natural selection, not immunity.
insight.aStarSignal: Separating three ideas that sound alike - antibody, antibiotic, resistance - and explaining a resistance graph with selection of alleles rather than immunity.
